morph.note: Imperative used in a deliberative question: ‘with what may there be a comparison?’, i.e. ‘what could it be compared with?’. The expected answer is ‘nothing’.
Neuter nom. sg. of a stem in -इन् (कारिन्): the n drops and the i stays short. अतिहारि is formed the same way.
Two subjects (कृपा and समरनिष्ठुरता) with a singular participle: it agrees with the nearer one, as often in verse.

mantras.anvaya: (हे) वरदे देवि, ते अस्य पराक्रमस्य उपमा केन भवतु? शत्रुभयकारि अतिहारि च रूपं कुत्र (अस्ति)? चित्ते कृपा समरनिष्ठुरता च भुवनत्रये अपि त्वयि एव दृष्टा।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two rhetorical questions (केन … भवतु; रूपं … कुत्र) and a statement with a passive participle (दृष्टा) whose place is त्वयि एव.
mantras.lit: With what can there be a comparison of this valour of yours? And where (is) a form fear-causing to enemies (and) exceedingly captivating? Compassion in the heart and relentlessness in battle are seen, O Devī, giver of boons, in you alone, even in the three worlds.
mantras.tr: To what could this valour of yours be compared? Where else is a form that strikes terror into enemies and yet captivates the heart? Compassion within and relentlessness in battle — in all three worlds, O Devī, giver of boons, these are seen together in you alone.
mantras.tr_note: ‘The heart’ after ‘captivates’ is supplied: अतिहारि means ‘exceedingly taking (the mind)’. ‘Together’ makes explicit what एव implies: the pair is found nowhere else.

comm.t: Nothing compares with her valour; no other form is at once terrible to enemies and supremely beautiful; nowhere in the three worlds are tenderness of heart and hardness in battle found together, except in her.

The verse names the paradox the hymn has been describing since 4.13: the gentle and the terrible, mercy and severity, held in one person. In the Śākta tradition this union of opposites is a mark of the supreme Goddess.

samasa.vigraha: सुराणाम् अरयः सुरारयः; उन्मदाः सुरारयः उन्मदसुरारयः; तेभ्यः भवम्
samasa.type: pañcamī tatpuruṣa (भव ‘arising’ as the final member) containing a karmadhāraya (उन्मदसुरारि) and a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (सुरारि)
samasa.literal: arising from the maddened foes of the gods
samasa.sense: the terror the frenzied asuras had caused
samasa.alt: उन्मद is itself a bahuvrīhi: उद्गतः मदः येषां ते, ‘in whom frenzy has risen’.

morph.note: Past participle of √त्रै ‘protect’: the root’s ai becomes ā before the suffix (त्रा + त → त्रात).
An absolutive in a passive sentence: its subject is the logical agent of the main verb नीताः, i.e. त्वया. ‘(You) having slain them, they were led (by you) to heaven.’
Past participle of अप + √अस् ‘throw’: ‘thrown away’, dispelled.
Two different words: in line 2, the pronoun तद् (m. nom. pl., ‘they’); in line 4, the enclitic of युष्मद् (dat. sg., ‘to you’).

mantras.anvaya: त्वया रिपुनाशनेन एतत् अखिलं त्रैलोक्यं त्रातम्; समरमूर्धनि हत्वा ते रिपुगणाः अपि (त्वया) दिवं नीताः; अस्माकम् उन्मदसुरारिभवं भयम् अपि अपास्तम्। ते नमः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three passive clauses with the one agent त्वया (त्रातम्, नीताः, अपास्तम्), then the salutation नमस्ते.
mantras.lit: This entire triple world has been saved by you through the destruction of the enemies; having slain (them) at the head of battle, they too, the hosts of enemies, have been led to heaven; and our fear, arising from the frenzied enemies of the gods, has been cast away. Salutation to you!
mantras.tr: By destroying the enemies you have saved these three worlds entire. Slaying them at the forefront of battle, you have led even those enemy hosts to heaven; and you have driven away our fear of the frenzied foes of the gods. Salutation to you!
mantras.tr_note: The passives (त्रातम्, नीताः, अपास्तम्) are turned into active sentences with ‘you’ as subject.

comm.t: The hymn sums up what the Goddess has done: the three worlds saved, the enemies themselves sent to heaven, and the gods’ fear removed. It closes the long vasantatilakā praise with नमस्ते.

Three beneficiaries are named in order, the world, the slain enemies and the gods, so the verse gathers the themes of 4.18–22. After the salutation the gods turn from praise to petition: the anuṣṭubh verses that follow (4.24–27) ask for protection.
